sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *aunque* "although" from A2 Unit 28 (*Fuimos al parque aunque hacía frío*), and *sin embargo* and *no obstante* from B1 Unit 1. The B2 point is that *aunque* takes two moods, and the mood tells the listener how you see the obstacle. With the indicative you state the obstacle as a fact: "although it is raining". With the subjunctive you do not state it: either it is only possible ("even if it rains") or you grant it for the sake of argument ("even if you are right") without letting it change anything.

sections.title: A fact or a possibility?
rows: Although it is raining, we're going out. (A fact: indicative.)
Even if it rains, we're going out. (A possibility: subjunctive.)
Although it's expensive, I'm buying it. (I know the price: indicative.)
Even if it's expensive, I'm buying it. (I don't know or don't care how much: subjunctive.)
Aunque tengas razón, no voy a cambiar de idea.
Even if you are right, I'm not going to change my mind. (A point granted: subjunctive.)
Es caro; sin embargo, lo compro.
It's expensive; however, I'm buying it. (Two sentences joined by a connector you know.)

sections.title: Which mood?
sections.content: Ask yourself one question: am I telling the listener that the obstacle is real, or am I only allowing for it? Real: indicative. Possible, or granted for the sake of argument: subjunctive. English helps here, because "although" goes with a fact and "even if" with a possibility. In the past, a real obstacle stays in the indicative (*aunque llovía*), and a possibility after a past verb uses the imperfect subjunctive from B1 Unit 38 (*Dijo que saldría aunque lloviera*).

items.spanish: Aunque tiene noventa años, todavía viaja solo.
items.english: Although he is ninety, he still travels alone.

items.spanish: Aunque cueste mucho dinero, voy a comprarlo.
items.english: Even if it costs a lot of money, I'm going to buy it.

items.spanish: Aunque llueva mañana, vamos al campo.
items.english: Even if it rains tomorrow, we're going to the country.

items.spanish: No voy a cambiar de idea aunque tengas razón.
items.english: I'm not going to change my mind even if you are right.

sections.content: *Sin embargo* and *no obstante* start a new clause after a full stop or a semicolon, with a comma after them. *Aunque* joins two clauses inside one sentence, and its clause can come first or last: *Aunque es caro, lo compro* and *Lo compro aunque es caro* mean the same.
